triage.name: Serum sickness
triage.reason: Fever, urticaria, arthralgias and lymphadenopathy days after a new drug; classic immune-complex reaction reachable by exposure history and exam.

exam: term 'Cardiac murmur' not found in SNOMED CT
exam: term 'Neurological examination normal' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Can occur at any age after exposure to the trigger

risk_factors.text: Recent exposure to a new medication, especially beta-lactam antibiotics
Exposure to foreign serum or antivenom
Prior sensitization to the same agent
Higher dose or longer duration of the offending drug

chief_complaints.text: I have a fever and a rash that started a few days ago

hpi.onset: Gradual, typically 1–2 weeks after starting the offending medication or exposure
hpi.duration: Symptoms usually last 1–2 weeks after stopping the trigger
hpi.progression: Fever and rash appear first, followed by joint pain and swelling; symptoms resolve gradually once the trigger is removed
hpi.location: Rash often starts on the trunk or at the injection site and spreads; joint pain is symmetric and affects multiple joints
hpi.quality: Rash is itchy and raised; joint pain is aching and stiff
hpi.severity: Moderate; fever can be high, joint pain can limit movement
hpi.timing: Continuous fever; rash and joint pain persist until the trigger is cleared

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the face or lips

pertinent_negatives: Recent tick bite or erythema migrans
Recent sore throat or streptococcal infection
Joint pain that is monoarticular or migratory
Rash that is petechial or purpuric
Recent travel to an area with endemic dengue or chikungunya
No new medication or foreign protein exposure

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

argues_against: Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs

positives.text: Swelling of the face or lips

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with fever, rash and irritability without clearly describing joint pain; lymphadenopathy and rash may be more prominent.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal relationship to a new medication

atypical.how_it_differs: Fever and rash may be less pronounced, and joint pain may be attributed to underlying osteoarthritis.
The immune-complex reaction may be blunted, with milder or atypical rash and less fever.

general.mild: Well-appearing, mildly uncomfortable, afebrile or low-grade fever, able to move about
general.moderate: Ill-appearing but not toxic, febrile, itchy and uncomfortable, moves cautiously because of joint pain
general.severe: Toxic-appearing, high fever, visibly distressed by itching and joint pain, prefers to lie still
general.critical: Very ill-appearing, diaphoretic, hypotensive or in respiratory distress from airway swelling

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the trunk, extremities and at the injection or exposure site
findings.finding: Raised, blanching, erythematous wheals that may coalesce and migrate

findings.maneuver: Stroke the skin firmly with a blunt object or fingernail
findings.finding: A raised linear wheal appears along the stroke line

findings.maneuver: Measure the temperature and assess for rigors or sweating
findings.finding: Elevated temperature, often with chills or sweats

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical, axillary and inguinal lymph node basins
findings.finding: Tender, enlarged, mobile lymph nodes, often generalized

findings.maneuver: Palpate and passively move the wrists, knees, ankles and small joints of the hands
findings.finding: Tenderness on palpation and with passive range of motion in multiple joints

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the affected joints for effusion or soft tissue swelling
findings.finding: Mild symmetric soft tissue swelling or effusion without deformity

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lips, tongue, periorbital area and oropharynx
findings.finding: Non-pitting swelling of the lips, eyelids or face

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen in all four quadrants
findings.finding: Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex and base

findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Listen over the neck and assess the voice and breathing
Inspect the skin for non-blanching lesions
Perform a brief neurologic screen including strength, sensation and cranial nerves
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss or cranial nerve abnormality

labs.caveat: Nonspecific; supports an inflammatory process but does not confirm serum sickness.
Nonspecific acute-phase reactant; useful for tracking but not diagnostic.
Mild leukocytosis is common; marked leukocytosis or left shift should prompt consideration of infection.
Eosinophilia is inconsistent and not required for diagnosis.
Mild thrombocytopenia can occur; severe thrombocytopenia suggests another diagnosis.
Rises with immune-complex glomerulonephritis; check urine for protein and blood if elevated.
Proteinuria suggests renal involvement; quantify with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio if present.
Hematuria with proteinuria raises concern for glomerulonephritis.

findings.text: Usually normal; no infiltrate, effusion or cardiomegaly
Normal valves and systolic function; no vegetation or pericardial effusion

initial.why: Assesses for leukocytosis, eosinophilia and thrombocytopenia
Checks renal function for immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Screens for proteinuria and hematuria from renal involvement
Adds an acute-phase marker and helps track response

supporting.only_if: renal or systemic features are prominent

supporting.why: Low C4 with low C3 further supports immune-complex disease
supporting.only_if: renal or systemic features are prominent

supporting.why: Looks for an alternative cause of fever and rash such as pneumonia
supporting.only_if: respiratory symptoms or hypoxia are present

supporting.why: Excludes endocarditis when a murmur or persistent fever is present
supporting.only_if: a new murmur or risk factors for endocarditis are present

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed unless infection is suspected
Not indicated for acute post-drug fever, rash and arthralgia
Not indicated for acute symmetric polyarthralgia without chronic synovitis
Not indicated for acute post-drug arthralgia
Rarely changes management; histology is nonspecific
No role in acute serum sickness

decision_points: Diagnosis is clinical: recent exposure to a drug or foreign protein plus fever, urticaria and arthralgia 1–2 weeks later
Stop the offending agent; symptoms usually resolve within 1–2 weeks
Check urine protein and creatinine to detect immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Consider infection (endocarditis, viral exanthem) when fever is high or a murmur is present

differential.name: Anaphylaxis
differential.why_considered: Both follow drug or foreign protein exposure and cause urticaria, angioedema and systemic symptoms.
differential.trigger: Urticaria with hypotension, wheeze, stridor or airway swelling minutes to hours after exposure

history: Onset within minutes to a few hours of exposure, not 1–2 weeks later
Rapidly progressive difficulty breathing or throat tightness
Prior immediate reaction to the same agent
exam: Hypotension or tachycardia disproportionate to fever
labs: Serum tryptase may be elevated acutely
No immune-complex features such as low complement
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal; no role in diagnosis

differential.name: Urticarial vasculitis
differential.why_considered: Persistent urticarial wheals with fever and arthralgia can mimic serum sickness.
differential.trigger: Individual wheals that last more than 24 hours, burn more than itch, and leave bruising or discoloration

history: Wheals persist in the same location for more than 24 hours
Lesions are painful or burning and may leave residual purpura or hyperpigmentation
Often no clear new drug exposure
exam: Wheals with purpuric or dusky centers
May have systemic findings such as renal or pulmonary involvement
labs: Urinalysis may show proteinuria or hematuria
imaging: Chest x-ray may show pulmonary involvement in hypocomplementemic disease

differential.name: Acute rheumatic fever
differential.why_considered: Fever, migratory polyarthritis and rash after a preceding infection.
differential.trigger: Migratory large-joint arthritis 2–4 weeks after pharyngitis, with evidence of recent streptococcal infection

history: Preceding sore throat 2–4 weeks earlier
Migratory arthritis of large joints
No new medication exposure
exam: Erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules or chorea
labs: Elevated or rising antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase B
Positive rapid streptococcal antigen or throat culture
imaging: Echocardiogram may show valvular regurgitation or thickening

differential.name: Infective endocarditis
differential.why_considered: Fever, rash and arthralgia with a new murmur can overlap with serum sickness.
differential.trigger: Persistent fever with a new murmur, embolic phenomena or risk factors such as injection drug use or prosthetic valves

history: Risk factors for bacteremia (injection drug use, indwelling lines, valvular disease)
Night sweats, weight loss, malaise over weeks
No temporal link to a new medication
exam: Splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes or Roth spots
labs: Urinalysis may show hematuria from immune-complex glomerulonephritis
imaging: Echocardiogram showing vegetations or valve destruction

differential.name: Viral exanthem
differential.why_considered: Fever and a widespread rash are common in viral illnesses and can be mistaken for a drug reaction.

history: Prodromal upper respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms
Sick contacts or seasonal pattern
Rash often maculopapular rather than urticarial
exam: Rash blanching and morbilliform rather than raised wheals
labs: Leukopenia or lymphocytosis rather than leukocytosis

differential.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
differential.why_considered: Fever, rash, arthralgia and lymphadenopathy with immune-complex features can resemble serum sickness.

history: Chronic or recurrent symptoms over months
Photosensitivity, oral ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon
No clear single new drug trigger

differential.name: Still disease (adult-onset)
differential.why_considered: High fever, evanescent rash and polyarthralgia are shared features.

history: Daily spiking fevers with a salmon-colored rash that appears with fever
Symptoms persist for weeks without a drug trigger
exam: Evanescent rash on trunk and extremities

differential.name: Disseminated gonococcal infection
differential.why_considered: Fever, rash and polyarthralgia in a sexually active patient.

history: New or multiple sexual partners
Migratory polyarthralgia with tenosynovitis
No new medication exposure
labs: Positive nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhea
Positive cultures from blood, joint or mucosal sites

severity.mild: Low-grade fever, limited urticaria and mild arthralgia; patient is comfortable and able to carry out daily activities.
severity.moderate: Prominent urticaria with itching, fever, symmetric polyarthralgia and lymphadenopathy; discomfort limits activity but no organ involvement.
severity.severe: High fever, extensive or coalescing urticaria, significant joint swelling, angioedema or evidence of renal involvement such as proteinuria or rising creatinine.
severity.critical: Airway compromise from angioedema, hypotension, or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with renal failure.

red_flags.meaning: Airway angioedema; risk of obstruction and need for immediate airway management.

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or tachycardia out of proportion to fever
red_flags.meaning: Anaphylaxis or severe systemic reaction; treat as an emergency.
Bronchospasm or pulmonary involvement; requires urgent assessment.

red_flags.finding: Gross hematuria, oliguria or rising creatinine
red_flags.meaning: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis; needs renal monitoring and possible referral.

red_flags.finding: Persistent high fever with a new murmur
red_flags.meaning: Consider infective endocarditis rather than serum sickness.

complications.name: Peripheral neuropathy
clues: Numbness, paresthesias or weakness in a limb

complications.name: Persistent arthralgia or joint stiffness
clues: Joint pain lasting beyond 2 weeks after stopping the trigger

special_populations.differences: May present with fever, rash and irritability without clearly localizing joint pain; lymphadenopathy and rash can be more prominent, and the temporal link to a new medication may be missed.
Fever and rash may be less pronounced, and joint pain may be attributed to underlying osteoarthritis; a lower threshold for checking renal function is reasonable.
The immune-complex reaction may be blunted, with milder or atypical rash and less fever, making the diagnosis harder to recognize.

Diagnosis and management are similar, but medication choices for symptom control must account for fetal safety; antihistamines and acetaminophen are generally preferred over NSAIDs, especially in the third trimester.
Baseline reduced renal function increases the risk and impact of immune-complex glomerulonephritis; monitor creatinine and urinalysis closely.

key_questions.question: Have you started any new medication in the last 1–3 weeks?
key_questions.looking_for: A new beta-lactam antibiotic, sulfonamide, or other drug started 1–2 weeks before symptoms; the key trigger

key_questions.question: Have you received any antivenom, foreign serum, or a monoclonal antibody infusion recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Exposure to foreign protein or biologic 1–2 weeks earlier

key_questions.question: When did the fever and rash start relative to the new medication?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset 1–2 weeks after starting the drug, not minutes to hours

key_questions.question: What does the rash look like, and is it itchy?
key_questions.looking_for: Raised, itchy, blanching wheals (urticaria) that may move around

key_questions.question: Do your joints hurt or feel swollen? Which ones?
key_questions.looking_for: Symmetric aching and stiffness in multiple joints, especially wrists, knees and ankles

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any swelling of your lips, tongue, face or throat?
key_questions.looking_for: Angioedema; airway involvement is an emergency

key_questions.question: Any trouble breathing, wheezing, or throat tightness?
key_questions.looking_for: Airway compromise or anaphylaxis rather than serum sickness

key_questions.question: Have you had a sore throat or strep infection in the past month?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent streptococcal infection suggesting acute rheumatic fever

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any tick bite or a spreading rash after a tick bite?
Any burning with urination, blood in the urine, or decreased urine output?
Have you had any weight loss, night sweats, or fevers over several weeks?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic systemic illness such as endocarditis or malignancy

key_questions.question: Have you ever had a reaction to this medication or a similar one before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior sensitization to the same agent

key_questions.question: Do you have any history of lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, or other autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Alternative chronic inflammatory or immune-complex disease

key_questions.question: Any new sexual partners or genital discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Disseminated gonococcal infection as an alternative cause of fever, rash and arthralgia

reasoning_points: New medication or foreign protein exposure 1–2 weeks before symptom onset
Fever with an itchy urticarial rash
Symptoms resolve after stopping the offending agent
Alternative diagnoses such as anaphylaxis, urticarial vasculitis, acute rheumatic fever, infective endocarditis and viral exanthem are considered and excluded
Renal function and urinalysis checked for immune-complex glomerulonephritis

easy: Clear new beta-lactam antibiotic started 1–2 weeks earlier
Classic triad of fever, urticaria and polyarthralgia
Symptoms improve after stopping the drug
medium: Trigger is a less obvious drug such as a sulfonamide, minocycline or bupropion
Prominent angioedema or abdominal pain without obvious rash
Older adult whose joint pain is attributed to osteoarthritis
Mild leukocytosis and elevated ESR with no clear source
hard: No clear medication history and the trigger is only found on careful review
Predominant renal involvement with proteinuria or rising creatinine
Child with fever, rash and irritability who cannot describe joint pain
Immunocompromised patient with blunted or atypical rash and fever
Overlap with urticarial vasculitis or early systemic lupus erythematosus
